Cross numbers and the characterization of finite abelian groups by length sets

Qinghai Zhong Address: Institute of Mathematics and Interdisciplinary Sciences, Xidian University, Xi’an 710126, China Email address: zhong@xidian.edu.cn
Abstract.

The Characterization Problem asks whether a finite abelian group with Davenport constant at least four is determined, up to isomorphism, by its system of length sets. This is a central inverse problem in non-unique factorization theory: it asks whether the possible numbers of irreducible factors retain enough information to recover the underlying class group. For rings of integers of algebraic number fields, an affirmative answer means that the ideal class group can be recovered from these factorization lengths alone. We resolve this problem for all homocyclic groups CnrC_{n}^{r}: if GG is a finite abelian group with 𝖣⁡(G)≥4\mathsf{D}(G)\geq 4 and ℒ⁡(G)=ℒ⁡(Cnr)\mathcal{L}(G)=\mathcal{L}(C_{n}^{r}), then G≅CnrG\cong C_{n}^{r}. The cross number of a sequence is the sum of the reciprocals of the orders of its terms. This weighted measure of sequence length links zero-sum theory with half-factoriality, and determining its maximal value for minimal zero-sum sequences is a longstanding extremal problem. We also obtain an exact formula for the maximal cross number of minimal zero-sum sequences over subsets whose minimum distance is divisible by the rank of the ambient group minus one. For G≅Cn1⊕⋯⊕CnrG\cong C_{n_{1}}\oplus\cdots\oplus C_{n_{r}} with 1<n1​∣⋯∣​nr1<n_{1}\mid\cdots\mid n_{r} and r≥max⁡{2,nr−2}r\geq\max\{2,n_{r}-2\}, we prove

𝖪⁡(G,r−1)=1+(r−1)​∑p|n1(1−p−𝗏p​(n1)),\mathsf{K}(G,r-1)=1+(r-1)\sum_{p\mid n_{1}}\left(1-p^{-\mathsf{v}_{p}(n_{1})}\right),

which is a key ingredient in resolving the Characterization Problem for homocyclic groups.

Key words and phrases: 
Finite abelian groups, length sets, cross numbers, Krull monoids, zero-sum sequences

11B30, 13F05, 20M13

1. Introduction and main results

Factorization theory has its origins in algebraic number theory, where the ideal class group measures the failure of unique factorization in rings of integers. A foundational result is Carlitz’s theorem of 1960: the ring of integers of an algebraic number field is half-factorial if and only if its class number is at most two. Thus even the requirement that all factorizations of each element have the same length detects a restriction on the class group. From the late 1980s onwards, the study of non-unique factorizations developed systematically in commutative monoids and integral domains. For an account of this development and the relation between arithmetical invariants and algebraic structure, see the survey [14].

A central invariant in this programme is the system of length sets. Let HH be an atomic monoid. For a nonunit a∈Ha\in H, the set 𝖫H​(a)\mathsf{L}_{H}(a) consists of the lengths of all factorizations of aa into atoms. The family ℒ⁡(H)={𝖫H​(a):a∈H}\mathcal{L}(H)=\{\mathsf{L}_{H}(a)\colon a\in H\} is the system of length sets of HH; for units, we set 𝖫H​(a)={0}\mathsf{L}_{H}(a)=\{0\}. Transfer homomorphisms connect the arithmetic of many rings and monoids with additive combinatorics. If HH is a transfer Krull monoid over a finite abelian group GG, then ℒ⁡(H)=ℒ⁡(G)\mathcal{L}(H)=\mathcal{L}(G), where ℒ⁡(G):=ℒ⁡(ℬ⁡(G))\mathcal{L}(G):=\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{B}(G)) is the system of length sets of the monoid ℬ⁡(G)\mathcal{B}(G) of zero-sum sequences over GG. Rings of integers of algebraic number fields are classical examples, with GG their ideal class group [4, 14].

The converse direction leads to the Characterization Problem: for finite abelian groups GG and G′G^{\prime} with 𝖣⁡(G)≥4\mathsf{D}(G)\geq 4, does

ℒ⁡(G)=ℒ⁡(G′)⟹G≅G′\mathcal{L}(G)=\mathcal{L}(G^{\prime})\quad\Longrightarrow\quad G\cong G^{\prime}

hold? Here 𝖣⁡(G)\mathsf{D}(G) is the Davenport constant of GG. This question belongs to the programme initiated by Narkiewicz in the 1970s of recovering class groups from arithmetical properties. Its significance is that length sets record only the possible numbers of irreducible factors, yet their full system is conjectured to determine the group up to isomorphism. The small-group restriction is necessary: for example, ℒ⁡(C3)=ℒ⁡(C22)\mathcal{L}(C_{3})=\mathcal{L}(C_{2}^{2}). For background on this problem, see [4, Section 6] and [14, Problem C], where it is formulated as a long-term problem in factorization theory.

Earlier progress is surveyed in [25]. Schmid established the characterization of Cn2C_{n}^{2} in [24], and Geroldinger and Schmid treated groups of rank two in [10]. Products of two atoms provide another source of characterizing information [1]. For homocyclic groups CnrC_{n}^{r}, that is, direct sums of rr cyclic groups of the same order nn, the work of Geroldinger and Zhong [13] and Zhong [28, 27] developed methods based on minimal distances and refined elasticities. In particular, Zhong proved the characterization for r≤n−3r\leq n-3, and for r≥n−1r\geq n-1 when nn is a prime power [27, Theorem 1.2]. The cases left open by these results are r=n−2r=n-2 and r≥n−1r\geq n-1 when nn is not a prime power.

A difficulty is that individual numerical invariants need not distinguish groups. For example, the largest minimal distance is max⁡{exp⁡(G)−2,𝗋⁡(G)−1}\max\{\exp(G)-2,\mathsf{r}(G)-1\}, so its value alone does not separate the contributions of the exponent and the rank. Zhong’s invariants ρ∗​(G,d)\rho^{*}(G,d) and 𝖪⁡(G,d)\mathsf{K}(G,d) combine restrictions on minimal distances with elasticity and cross numbers [27]. These invariants provide finer information about the integers n1,…,nrn_{1},\ldots,n_{r} in the decomposition G≅Cn1⊕⋯⊕CnrG\cong C_{n_{1}}\oplus\cdots\oplus C_{n_{r}} with 1<n1​∣⋯∣​nr1<n_{1}\mid\cdots\mid n_{r}. For related work on transfer Krull monoids and elasticity, see [11, 15, 16]; general background is provided by [8, 9, 7].

Cross numbers have a history closely tied to these arithmetical questions. Introduced by Krause in 1984 in the study of algebraic number fields [20], and developed by Krause and Zahlten for Krull monoids [21], the cross number of a sequence S=g1⋅…⋅gℓS=g_{1}\cdot\ldots\cdot g_{\ell} is

𝗄⁡(S)=∑i=1ℓ1ord⁡(gi).\mathsf{k}(S)=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\frac{1}{\ord(g_{i})}.

The Davenport constant is the maximum length of a minimal zero-sum sequence. The maximal cross number is the corresponding weighted maximum, with each term gg assigned weight 1/ord⁡(g)1/\ord(g). The cross-number criterion for half-factoriality gives a direct connection with factorization theory: a subset G0G_{0} of a finite abelian group is half-factorial if and only if every atom over G0G_{0} has cross number one [8]. More generally, cross numbers allow one to compare factorization lengths by using an additive weight on zero-sum sequences. Determining the structure of minimal zero-sum sequences attaining the maximal cross number is an associated inverse problem in additive combinatorics [6].

Determining the maximal cross number 𝖪⁡(G)\mathsf{K}(G) is a difficult extremal problem. If G≅⨁i=1tCqiG\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^{t}C_{q_{i}}, where each qiq_{i} is a prime power, the classical cross-number conjecture predicts

𝖪⁡(G)=1exp⁡(G)+∑i=1t(1−1qi).\mathsf{K}(G)=\frac{1}{\exp(G)}+\sum_{i=1}^{t}\left(1-\frac{1}{q_{i}}\right).

The right-hand side is attained by an explicit construction; the difficulty is to prove the matching upper bound for arbitrary minimal zero-sum sequences [21, 19]. The formula holds for pp-groups [5], while subsequent work has treated further families and developed bounds and structural methods [6, 18, 19]. For groups with several prime divisors, projecting a minimal zero-sum sequence to its primary components need not preserve minimality, which obstructs a direct reduction to the pp-group case. The invariant considered here restricts the cross-number problem to subsets satisfying a condition on their minimum distance. Its exact value can then be used, through refined elasticities, to recover information about the cyclic factors of the group.

We study the invariant 𝖪⁡(G,d)\mathsf{K}(G,d) introduced in [27, Definition 3.3]. It is the largest cross number of an atom over a subset whose set of distances is nonempty and has minimum divisible by dd. Precise definitions are given in Section 2. Our first result determines this invariant at d=𝗋⁡(G)−1d=\mathsf{r}(G)-1 when the rank is at least exp⁡(G)−2\exp(G)-2. The formula shows that, in this range, the invariant depends only on the rank rr and the order n1n_{1} of the smallest cyclic factor in the displayed decomposition.

Theorem 1.1.

Let G≅Cn1⊕⋯⊕CnrG\cong C_{n_{1}}\oplus\cdots\oplus C_{n_{r}} be a finite abelian group with 1<n1​∣⋯∣​nr1<n_{1}\mid\cdots\mid n_{r} and r≥max⁡{2,nr−2}r\geq\max\{2,n_{r}-2\}. Then

𝖪⁡(G,r−1)=1+(r−1)​∑p|n1(1−1p𝗏p​(n1)),\mathsf{K}(G,r-1)=1+(r-1)\sum_{p\mid n_{1}}\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{\mathsf{v}_{p}(n_{1})}}\right),

where the sum runs over the distinct prime divisors of n1n_{1}.

For G=CnrG=C_{n}^{r} and r≥n−1r\geq n-1, Theorem 1.1 proves Conjecture 5.1, C2, of [27]. It also proves C1: letting s=n​∑p|n(1−p−𝗏p​(n))s=n\sum_{p\mid n}(1-p^{-\mathsf{v}_{p}(n)}), one has gcd⁡(s,n)=1\gcd(s,n)=1. Indeed, for each prime p|np\mid n, the integer ss is congruent to −n/p𝗏p​(n)-n/p^{\mathsf{v}_{p}(n)} modulo pp. Our second result resolves the Characterization Problem for homocyclic finite abelian groups.

Theorem 1.2.

Let n≥2n\geq 2 and r≥1r\geq 1 be integers, and let GG be a finite abelian group with 𝖣⁡(G)≥4\mathsf{D}(G)\geq 4. If ℒ⁡(G)=ℒ⁡(Cnr)\mathcal{L}(G)=\mathcal{L}(C_{n}^{r}), then G≅CnrG\cong C_{n}^{r}.

Zhong proved the assertion when r≤n−3r\leq n-3, and also when r≥n−1r\geq n-1 and nn is a prime power [27, Theorem 1.2]. Theorem 1.1, together with [27, Proposition 5.2], gives the result for r≥n−1r\geq n-1. The remaining case is r=n−2r=n-2. For n≥6n\geq 6, we compare ρ∗​(G,n−3)\rho^{*}(G,n-3) with the corresponding invariant of Cnn−2C_{n}^{n-2}; the cases n∈{4,5}n\in\{4,5\} are treated separately.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the notation and collects the preliminary results. Section 3 establishes the cross-number formula in Theorem 1.1. Sections 4 and 5 develop the structural results and elasticity comparisons used in Section 6 to prove Theorem 1.2. Finally, Section 7 presents further questions.

2. Background on zero-sum sequences and length sets

We fix our notation and recall the definitions needed in the sequel. For general background on zero-sum sequences and factorization theory, we refer to [8, 9, 7].

We denote by ℕ\mathbb{N} the set of positive integers and set ℕ0=ℕ∪{0}\mathbb{N}_{0}=\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}. For integers a≤ba\leq b, we write [a,b]={k∈ℤ:a≤k≤b}[a,b]=\{k\in\mathbb{Z}:a\leq k\leq b\}. For a prime pp and m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N}, let 𝗏p​(m)\mathsf{v}_{p}(m) denote the pp-adic valuation of mm.

Throughout, groups are written additively. Let GG be a nontrivial finite abelian group, and write

G≅Cn1⊕⋯⊕Cnr, with 1<n1​∣⋯∣​nr,G\cong C_{n_{1}}\oplus\cdots\oplus C_{n_{r}},\qquad\text{ with }\quad 1<n_{1}\mid\cdots\mid n_{r},

where CmC_{m} denotes a cyclic group of order mm. We denote by 𝗋⁡(G)=r\mathsf{r}(G)=r and exp⁡(G)=nr\exp(G)=n_{r} the rank and exponent of GG, respectively. For g∈Gg\in G, let ord⁡(g)\ord(g) denote its order; in particular, ord⁡(0)=1\ord(0)=1. For a prime pp, we denote by GpG_{p} the pp-primary component of GG and by πp:G→Gp\pi_{p}:G\to G_{p} the canonical projection. For an integer mm and a subset A⊂GA\subset G, we set m⋅A={m​a:a∈A}m\cdot A=\{ma:a\in A\}.

Let G0⊂GG_{0}\subset G. We denote by ℱ⁡(G0)\mathcal{F}(G_{0}) the multiplicatively written free abelian monoid with basis G0G_{0}. Its elements are finite unordered sequences over G0G_{0}, with repetitions allowed. For a sequence

S=g1⋅…⋅gℓ=∏g∈G0g𝗏g​(S)∈ℱ⁡(G0),S=g_{1}\cdot\ldots\cdot g_{\ell}=\prod_{g\in G_{0}}g^{\mathsf{v}_{g}(S)}\in\mathcal{F}(G_{0}),

we denote by 𝗏g​(S)\mathsf{v}_{g}(S) the multiplicity of gg in SS and set

|S|=ℓ,supp⁡(S)={g∈G0:𝗏g​(S)>0},σ⁡(S)=g1+…+gℓ=∑g∈G0𝗏g​(S)​g.|S|=\ell,\qquad\supp(S)=\{g\in G_{0}:\mathsf{v}_{g}(S)>0\},\qquad\sigma(S)=g_{1}+\ldots+g_{\ell}=\sum_{g\in G_{0}}\mathsf{v}_{g}(S)g.

The identity element 1=1ℱ⁡(G0)1=1_{\mathcal{F}(G_{0})} is the trivial sequence with |1|=0|1|=0 and σ⁡(1)=0\sigma(1)=0. We call a sequence squarefree if each of its terms has multiplicity one. We write T|ST\mid S if TT is a subsequence of SS. In this case, we write S​T−1ST^{-1} for the sequence obtained by deleting TT from SS. We call SS a zero-sum sequence if σ⁡(S)=0\sigma(S)=0, and zero-sum free if it has no nontrivial zero-sum subsequence. The monoid of zero-sum sequences over G0G_{0} is

ℬ⁡(G0)={S∈ℱ⁡(G0):σ⁡(S)=0}.\mathcal{B}(G_{0})=\{S\in\mathcal{F}(G_{0}):\sigma(S)=0\}.

Its atoms (or irreducibles) are the minimal zero-sum sequences, that is, the nontrivial zero-sum sequences having no proper nontrivial zero-sum subsequence. We set 𝒜⁡(G0):=𝒜⁡(ℬ⁡(G0))\mathcal{A}(G_{0}):=\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{B}(G_{0})) and denote by 𝖣⁡(G)=max⁡{|U|:U∈𝒜⁡(G)}\mathsf{D}(G)=\max\{|U|:U\in\mathcal{A}(G)\} the Davenport constant of GG.

For B∈ℬ⁡(G0)B\in\mathcal{B}(G_{0}), we denote by 𝖫⁡(B)\mathsf{L}(B) its length set. Thus k∈𝖫⁡(B)k\in\mathsf{L}(B) if and only if BB has a factorization into kk atoms, and 𝖫⁡(1)={0}\mathsf{L}(1)=\{0\} by convention. We set

ℒ⁡(G0):=ℒ⁡(ℬ⁡(G0))={𝖫⁡(B):B∈ℬ⁡(G0)}.\mathcal{L}(G_{0}):=\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{B}(G_{0}))=\{\mathsf{L}(B):B\in\mathcal{B}(G_{0})\}.

We call G0G_{0} half-factorial if every length set in ℒ⁡(G0)\mathcal{L}(G_{0}) is a singleton. For a finite nonempty set L⊂ℕL\subset\mathbb{N}, we set the elasticity ρ⁡(L)=max⁡L/min⁡L\rho(L)=\max L/\min L, and set ρ⁡({0})=1\rho(\{0\})=1. For B∈ℬ⁡(G0)B\in\mathcal{B}(G_{0}), its elasticity is ρ⁡(𝖫⁡(B))\rho(\mathsf{L}(B)). For G0≠∅G_{0}\neq\emptyset, we set

ρ⁡(G0)=sup{ρ⁡(𝖫⁡(B)):B∈ℬ⁡(G0)},\rho(G_{0})=\sup\left\{\rho(\mathsf{L}(B))\colon B\in\mathcal{B}(G_{0})\right\},

and set ρ⁡(∅)=1\rho(\emptyset)=1. For the empty subset, we have ℱ⁡(∅)=ℬ⁡(∅)={1}\mathcal{F}(\emptyset)=\mathcal{B}(\emptyset)=\{1\}, ℒ⁡(∅)={{0}}\mathcal{L}(\emptyset)=\{\{0\}\}, and Δ⁡(∅)=∅\Delta(\emptyset)=\emptyset.

For S∈ℱ⁡(G0)S\in\mathcal{F}(G_{0}), its cross number is

𝗄⁡(S)=∑g∈G0𝗏g​(S)ord⁡(g).\mathsf{k}(S)=\sum_{g\in G_{0}}\frac{\mathsf{v}_{g}(S)}{\ord(g)}.

For G0≠∅G_{0}\neq\emptyset, we set

𝖪⁡(G0)=max⁡{𝗄⁡(U):U∈𝒜⁡(G0)}.\mathsf{K}(G_{0})=\max\{\mathsf{k}(U):U\in\mathcal{A}(G_{0})\}.

We call G0G_{0} a large cross number set (an LCN-set) if every atom over G0G_{0} has cross number at least one. For cross-number invariants and half-factorial subsets, see [21, 18, 19, 3, 22, 23].

For a finite set L⊂ℤL\subset\mathbb{Z}, let Δ⁡(L)\Delta(L) denote the set of positive differences between consecutive elements of LL. We set

Δ⁡(G0):=Δ⁡(ℬ⁡(G0))=⋃B∈ℬ⁡(G0)Δ⁡(𝖫⁡(B))\Delta(G_{0}):=\Delta(\mathcal{B}(G_{0}))=\bigcup_{B\in\mathcal{B}(G_{0})}\Delta(\mathsf{L}(B))

and

Δ∗(G)={minΔ(G0):G0⊂G,Δ(G0)≠∅}.\Delta^{*}(G)=\{\min\Delta(G_{0}):G_{0}\subset G,\ \Delta(G_{0})\neq\emptyset\}.

We call Δ⁡(G0)\Delta(G_{0}) the set of distances of G0G_{0} and Δ∗​(G)\Delta^{*}(G) the set of minimal distances of GG. If Δ⁡(G0)≠∅\Delta(G_{0})\neq\emptyset, then min⁡Δ⁡(G0)\min\Delta(G_{0}) is the minimum distance of G0G_{0}. In particular, G0G_{0} is half-factorial if and only if Δ⁡(G0)=∅\Delta(G_{0})=\emptyset. We denote by 𝗆⁡(G)\mathsf{m}(G) the largest minimum distance of a non-half-factorial LCN-subset of GG, and set 𝗆⁡(G)=0\mathsf{m}(G)=0 if no such subset exists. For results on distances and minimal distances, see [26, 12, 17, 28].

We denote by Δ1​(G)\Delta_{1}(G) the set of all d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N} for which ℒ⁡(G)\mathcal{L}(G) contains arbitrarily long almost arithmetic progressions of difference dd with a common bound, in the sense of [27, Section 2]. For d∈Δ1​(G)d\in\Delta_{1}(G), define

𝖪(G,d)=max{𝖪(G0):G0⊂G,Δ(G0)≠∅,d∣minΔ(G0)}\mathsf{K}(G,d)=\max\{\mathsf{K}(G_{0}):G_{0}\subset G,\ \Delta(G_{0})\neq\emptyset,\ d\mid\min\Delta(G_{0})\}

and

ρ∗(G,d)=max{ρ(G0):G0⊂G,Δ(G0)≠∅,d∣minΔ(G0)}.\rho^{*}(G,d)=\max\{\rho(G_{0}):G_{0}\subset G,\ \Delta(G_{0})\neq\emptyset,\ d\mid\min\Delta(G_{0})\}.

These maxima are taken over nonempty families [27, Definition 3.3]. Thus ρ∗​(G,d)\rho^{*}(G,d) is the largest elasticity of a non-half-factorial subset whose minimum distance is divisible by dd; 𝖪⁡(G,d)\mathsf{K}(G,d) is the corresponding maximum of the cross numbers of atoms over such subsets.

We collect the results used in the proofs below.

Lemma 2.1.

Let G≅Cn1⊕⋯⊕CnrG\cong C_{n_{1}}\oplus\cdots\oplus C_{n_{r}}, where 1<n1​∣⋯∣​nr1<n_{1}\mid\cdots\mid n_{r}.

  1. 1.

    If |G|≥3|G|\geq 3, then ρ⁡(G)=𝖣⁡(G)/2\rho(G)=\mathsf{D}(G)/2 and 𝖣⁡(G)≥1+∑i=1r(ni−1)\mathsf{D}(G)\geq 1+\sum_{i=1}^{r}(n_{i}-1).

  2. 2.

    If GG is a pp-group, then 𝖣⁡(G)=1+∑i=1r(ni−1)\mathsf{D}(G)=1+\sum_{i=1}^{r}(n_{i}-1) and 𝖪⁡(G)=1/exp⁡(G)+∑i=1r(1−1/ni)\mathsf{K}(G)=1/\exp(G)+\sum_{i=1}^{r}(1-1/n_{i}).

  3. 3.

    A nonempty subset G0⊂GG_{0}\subset G is half-factorial if and only if 𝗄⁡(U)=1\mathsf{k}(U)=1 for every U∈𝒜⁡(G0)U\in\mathcal{A}(G_{0}).

Proof.

See [8, Sections 5 and 6] and [27, Lemmas 2.1 and 2.2]. ∎

Lemma 2.2.

Let GG be a finite abelian group with |G|≥3|G|\geq 3.

  1. 1.

    For every non-half-factorial subset G0⊂GG_{0}\subset G, we have

    min⁡Δ⁡(G0)=gcd⁡Δ⁡(G0).\min\Delta(G_{0})=\gcd\Delta(G_{0}).
  2. 2.

    We have Δ∗(G)⊂Δ1(G)⊂{d∈Δ(G): there exists d∗∈Δ∗(G) such that d∣d∗}\Delta^{*}(G)\subset\Delta_{1}(G)\subset\{d\in\Delta(G)\colon\text{ there exists }d^{*}\in\Delta^{*}(G)\text{ such that }d\mid d^{*}\} and

    max⁡Δ1​(G)=max⁡Δ∗​(G)=max⁡{exp⁡(G)−2,𝗋⁡(G)−1}.\max\Delta_{1}(G)=\max\Delta^{*}(G)=\max\{\exp(G)-2,\mathsf{r}(G)-1\}.

    Moreover,

    𝗆⁡(G)≤max⁡{𝗋⁡(G)−1,⌊exp⁡(G)/2⌋−1}.\mathsf{m}(G)\leq\max\{\mathsf{r}(G)-1,\lfloor\exp(G)/2\rfloor-1\}.
  3. 3.

    If e1,…,ese_{1},\ldots,e_{s} are independent elements of the same order m≥2m\geq 2, where s≥2s\geq 2, then

    min⁡Δ⁡({e1,…,es,e1+⋯+es})=s−1.\min\Delta(\{e_{1},\ldots,e_{s},e_{1}+\cdots+e_{s}\})=s-1.

    In particular, if 𝗋⁡(G)≥2\mathsf{r}(G)\geq 2, then [1,𝗋⁡(G)−1]⊂Δ∗​(G)[1,\mathsf{r}(G)-1]\subset\Delta^{*}(G).

Proof.

See [8, Propositions 1.4.4 and 6.8.2] for Items 1 and 3.

2. The inclusion Δ∗​(G)⊂Δ1​(G)\Delta^{*}(G)\subset\Delta_{1}(G) follows from [8, Corollary 4.3.16] and the other assertions follow from [17, Theorem 1.1] and [28, Proposition 3.7]. ∎

Lemma 2.3.

Suppose GG and G′G^{\prime} are finite abelian groups with 𝖣⁡(G)≥4\mathsf{D}(G)\geq 4 and ℒ⁡(G)=ℒ⁡(G′)\mathcal{L}(G)=\mathcal{L}(G^{\prime}). Then 𝖣⁡(G)=𝖣⁡(G′)\mathsf{D}(G)=\mathsf{D}(G^{\prime}), Δ1​(G)=Δ1​(G′)\Delta_{1}(G)=\Delta_{1}(G^{\prime}), and ρ∗​(G,d)=ρ∗​(G′,d)\rho^{*}(G,d)=\rho^{*}(G^{\prime},d) for every d∈Δ1​(G)d\in\Delta_{1}(G). In particular,

max⁡{exp⁡(G)−2,𝗋⁡(G)−1}=max⁡{exp⁡(G′)−2,𝗋⁡(G′)−1}.\max\{\exp(G)-2,\mathsf{r}(G)-1\}=\max\{\exp(G^{\prime})-2,\mathsf{r}(G^{\prime})-1\}.

If either group is isomorphic to a subgroup of the other, then G≅G′G\cong G^{\prime}.

Proof.

The assertion 𝖣⁡(G)=𝖣⁡(G′)\mathsf{D}(G)=\mathsf{D}(G^{\prime}) follows from [8, Proposition 7.3.1.3] and the other assertions follow from [27, Proposition 3.5 and Lemma 4.1]. ∎

Lemma 2.4.

Let GG be a finite abelian group with exp⁡(G)≥3\exp(G)\geq 3, and let G0⊂GG_{0}\subset G be non-half-factorial with min⁡Δ⁡(G0)≥⌊exp⁡(G)/2⌋\min\Delta(G_{0})\geq\lfloor\exp(G)/2\rfloor.

  1. 1.

    An atom U∈𝒜⁡(G0)U\in\mathcal{A}(G_{0}) with 𝗄⁡(U)<1\mathsf{k}(U)<1 is squarefree, all its terms have order exp⁡(G)\exp(G), and |U|=exp⁡(G)−min⁡Δ⁡(G0)|U|=\exp(G)-\min\Delta(G_{0}).

  2. 2.

    If U∈𝒜⁡(G0)U\in\mathcal{A}(G_{0}) is an atom with 𝗄⁡(U)≥1\mathsf{k}(U)\geq 1, then its support is an LCN-set. If its support is non-half-factorial, then min⁡Δ⁡(supp⁡(U))≤|supp⁡(U)|−2\min\Delta(\supp(U))\leq|\supp(U)|-2.

  3. 3.

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

Note that r≥2r\geq 2. If (nr,r)=(4,2)(n_{r},r)=(4,2), then GG is either C2⊕C4C_{2}\oplus C_{4} or C42C_{4}^{2}. Suppose nr≥6n_{r}\geq 6. Since r≥nr−2≥⌊nr/2⌋+1r\geq n_{r}-2\geq\lfloor n_{r}/2\rfloor+1, Lemma 2.5.2 gives

𝖪⁡(G,r−1)≥1+(r−1)​∑p|n1(1−1p𝗏p​(n1)).\mathsf{K}(G,r-1)\geq 1+(r-1)\sum_{p\mid n_{1}}\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{\mathsf{v}_{p}(n_{1})}}\right).

𝗄⁡(A)≤1+(r−1)​∑p|n1(1−1p𝗏p​(n1)).\mathsf{k}(A)\leq 1+(r-1)\sum_{p\mid n_{1}}\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{\mathsf{v}_{p}(n_{1})}}\right).

We may assume that 𝗄⁡(A)>1\mathsf{k}(A)>1. In view of r≥nr−2≥⌊nr/2⌋+1r\geq n_{r}-2\geq\lfloor n_{r}/2\rfloor+1, it follows from Lemma 2.4.2 that supp⁡(A)\supp(A) is an LCN-set. By Lemma 2.2.1 and 2, we have min⁡Δ⁡(G0)\min\Delta(G_{0}) divides min⁡Δ⁡(supp⁡(A))\min\Delta(\supp(A)) and min⁡Δ⁡(supp⁡(A))≤max⁡{r−1,nr−2}<2​(r−1)\min\Delta(\supp(A))\leq\max\{r-1,n_{r}-2\}<2(r-1), whence min⁡Δ⁡(supp⁡(A))=r−1\min\Delta(\supp(A))=r-1. In view of r≥nr−2≥4r\geq n_{r}-2\geq 4, the assertion now follows from Proposition 3.3. ∎

4. Subsets with minimum distance exp⁡(G)−3\exp(G)-3

In this section, we consider subsets with minimum distance exp⁡(G)−3\exp(G)-3. Every atom of cross number less than one over such a subset has three distinct terms. The following lemmas describe the subgroup they generate and its intersection with the subgroup generated by the remaining support.

Lemma 4.1.

Let G=H⊕KG=H\oplus K be a finite abelian group and let G0⊂GG_{0}\subset G be a subset.

  1. 1.

    If GG is a pp-group and H∩⟨G0⟩≠0H\cap\langle G_{0}\rangle\neq 0, then there exists a subset E⊂G0E\subset G_{0} with |E|≤𝗋⁡(K)+1|E|\leq\mathsf{r}(K)+1 such that H∩⟨E⟩≠0H\cap\langle E\rangle\neq 0.

  2. 2.

    If G∗G^{*} is a subgroup of GG such that G∗≅Cexp⁡(G)sG^{*}\cong C_{\exp(G)}^{s} for some s∈ℕs\in\mathbb{N}, then G∗G^{*} is a direct summand.

Proof.

1. Let φK:G→K\varphi_{K}\colon G\to K be the projection, and set M=⟨φK​(G0)⟩M=\langle\varphi_{K}(G_{0})\rangle. A generating set of a finite abelian pp-group contains a generating subset of size at most its rank. Thus there exists E∗⊂G0E^{*}\subset G_{0} with |E∗|≤𝗋⁡(M)≤𝗋⁡(K)|E^{*}|\leq\mathsf{r}(M)\leq\mathsf{r}(K) such that ⟨φK​(E∗)⟩=M\langle\varphi_{K}(E^{*})\rangle=M. In particular, G0⊂H+⟨E∗⟩G_{0}\subset H+\langle E^{*}\rangle. If H∩⟨E∗⟩≠0H\cap\langle E^{*}\rangle\neq 0, take E=E∗E=E^{*}. Otherwise H+⟨E∗⟩=H⊕⟨E∗⟩H+\langle E^{*}\rangle=H\oplus\langle E^{*}\rangle. Since H∩⟨G0⟩≠0H\cap\langle G_{0}\rangle\neq 0, some g∈G0g\in G_{0} lies outside ⟨E∗⟩\langle E^{*}\rangle. Write g=h+ug=h+u with h∈Hh\in H and u∈⟨E∗⟩u\in\langle E^{*}\rangle. Then

0≠h∈H∩⟨E∗∪{g}⟩.0\neq h\in H\cap\langle E^{*}\cup\{g\}\rangle.

Thus E=E∗∪{g}E=E^{*}\cup\{g\} has the required size.

2. The assertion follows by applying Szele’s splitting criterion [2, Chapter 5, Lemma 2.1] to each primary component of GG. ∎

Lemma 4.2.

  1. 1.

Since min⁡Δ⁡({e1,…,eN−1,g,−g})=N−2=𝗋⁡(⟨E⟩)−1\min\Delta(\{e_{1},\ldots,e_{N-1},g,-g\})=N-2=\mathsf{r}(\langle E\rangle)-1 and NN is not a prime power, Proposition 5.2.2 gives

ρ⁡(G0)≤ρ∗​(⟨E⟩,N−2)=𝖪⁡(⟨E⟩,N−2)≤𝖪⁡(G,N−2).\rho(G_{0})\leq\rho^{*}(\langle E\rangle,N-2)=\mathsf{K}(\langle E\rangle,N-2)\leq\mathsf{K}(G,N-2).

∎

7. Concluding remarks and further problems

Theorem 1.1 determines 𝖪⁡(G,r−1)\mathsf{K}(G,r-1) when r≥max⁡{2,exp⁡(G)−2}r\geq\max\{2,\exp(G)-2\}. In this range, its value depends only on the rank and the order of the smallest cyclic factor in the decomposition G≅Cn1⊕⋯⊕CnrG\cong C_{n_{1}}\oplus\cdots\oplus C_{n_{r}} with 1<n1​∣⋯∣​nr1<n_{1}\mid\cdots\mid n_{r}. Theorem 1.2 resolves the Characterization Problem for homocyclic finite abelian groups with Davenport constant at least four. We conclude with three related questions.

1. Characterization beyond homocyclic groups. The general Characterization Problem asks whether

ℒ⁡(G)=ℒ⁡(G′)⟹G≅G′\mathcal{L}(G)=\mathcal{L}(G^{\prime})\quad\Longrightarrow\quad G\cong G^{\prime}

for finite abelian groups G,G′G,G^{\prime} with 𝖣⁡(G)≥4\mathsf{D}(G)\geq 4 [25, 27, 7]. The groups Cm⊕CnrC_{m}\oplus C_{n}^{r}, where 1<m<n1<m<n and m|nm\mid n, provide a natural family in which to extend the present results. For which of these groups can comparisons of refined elasticities determine mm, nn, and rr? More generally, which integers in the decomposition of a finite abelian group into cyclic factors can be recovered from its refined elasticities?

2. Cross numbers at smaller ranks and distances. Let G≅Cn1⊕⋯⊕CnrG\cong C_{n_{1}}\oplus\cdots\oplus C_{n_{r}} with 1<n1​∣⋯∣​nr1<n_{1}\mid\cdots\mid n_{r} and 2≤r<exp⁡(G)−22\leq r<\exp(G)-2. Determine 𝖪⁡(G,r−1)\mathsf{K}(G,r-1) and identify the groups for which the formula in Theorem 1.1 remains valid. One may also ask for 𝖪⁡(G,d)\mathsf{K}(G,d) when d∈Δ1​(G)d\in\Delta_{1}(G) and d<r−1d<r-1. Under the hypotheses of Lemma 2.5.1, the denominator of 𝗄⁡(U)−1\mathsf{k}(U)-1 divides nr−dn_{r-d} for every atom UU of cross number greater than one over a subset whose minimum distance is divisible by dd. Can this restriction be combined with estimates for the primary components to determine further values of 𝖪⁡(G,d)\mathsf{K}(G,d)? The argument in Section 3 also uses Lemma 3.1, whose hypothesis is min⁡Δ⁡(G0)≥exp⁡(G)−3\min\Delta(G_{0})\geq\exp(G)-3. Bounds for the maximum of the factorization lengths under weaker hypotheses may allow the same approach at smaller distances.

3. Equality of refined elasticity and cross number. For every d∈Δ1​(G)d\in\Delta_{1}(G), we have ρ∗​(G,d)≥𝖪⁡(G,d)\rho^{*}(G,d)\geq\mathsf{K}(G,d). Propositions 5.1, 5.2, and 5.4 establish equality in several cases, while Proposition 5.2 also records a family with strict inequality. Determine further pairs (G,d)(G,d) for which equality holds. The structural arguments in Sections 4 and 5 concern atoms of cross number less than one at minimum distances exp⁡(G)−3\exp(G)-3 and exp⁡(G)−2\exp(G)-2, respectively. Their supports have three and two elements. More generally, Lemma 2.4.1 determines their lengths when the minimum distance is at least ⌊exp⁡(G)/2⌋\lfloor\exp(G)/2\rfloor. Descriptions of the subgroups generated by larger supports, and of their intersections with the subgroups generated by the remaining elements, may yield further elasticity comparisons and applications to the Characterization Problem.
